decisions.location: Section 1 Introduction, p. 2, lines 76-84 (and References, p. 12, lines 507-510)
decisions.quote:
A recent study by Riccucci et al. (2016) indicates that symbolic gender representation is an important quality for
citizen–state interactions. Increasing the representation of female officials positively affected the willingness to
co-produce in a recycling initiative. The results suggest that women were more willing to co-produce when encountering higher shares of female officials. These findings promise considerable benefits for public organizations, as
symbolic representation may lead to better services as well as cost savings (Riccucci & Van Ryzin, 2017). However,
Van Ryzin et al. (2017) conducted a recent replication with a different policy context that could not confirm the
findings. Symbolic representation did not unfold in the context of emergency preparation.
Consequently, Van Ryzin et al. (2017) proposed additional replication studies “as an opportunity to further
develop and test the underlying theory of symbolic representation to more deeply probe its mechanisms and contingencies” (p. 1376). Following this notion, the present study provides a wide replication (Walker et al., 2019) of the
original research by Riccucci et al. (2016).
decisions.reason: Shipped row 540 pairs Sievert (2021, DOI: 10.1111/padm.12743) with Riccucci & Van Ryzin (2017, Public Administration Review 77(1), 21-30, early view 2016, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12649, 'Representative Bureaucracy: A Lever to Enhance Social Equity, Coproduction, and Democracy'). In the primary text, Riccucci & Van Ryzin (2017) is cited exclusively as conceptual and theoretical background on symbolic representation (lines 72-73, 78-79, 109-112, 129-132, 344; reference at lines 509-510). The sole empirical study re-tested by Sievert (2021) is the recycling survey experiment of Riccucci, Van Ryzin, & Li (2016, Public Administration Review 76(1), 121-130, early view 2015, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12401, 'Representative Bureaucracy and the Willingness to Coproduce: An Experimental Study'), which is already represented in shipped sibling row 541 (paired with blind target 0). Because 10.1111/puar.12649 is an untested conceptual background citation and the true empirical target is already in row 541, blind coding rightly omitted 10.1111/puar.12649 and row 540 must be removed.

decisions.quote: The replication's results do not confirm the findings outlined by Riccucci et al. (2016). In the present study, symbolic gender representation does not affect the willingness to co-produce. Equivalence testing (Lakens, 2017) indicates null findings based on the absence of meaningful treatment effects.
decisions.reason: Under Codebook Step 3 ('STEP 3 — OUTCOME, per original' and 'SEVERAL ORIGINALS: WHICH TARGETS A VERDICT COVERS: A target the paper's words never place inside such a verdict, and never discuss on its own, is "cannot_be_determined" — on every outcome field asked for above. Do not carry one target's outcome across to another') and FIELD_REVIEW_INSTRUCTIONS.md ('For undeterminable use null... Resolve dependencies explicitly; do not silently borrow another target's outcome'), outcome is strictly target-specific. Because row 540's shipped target (Riccucci & Van Ryzin, 2017, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12649) is a non-tested conceptual background paper resolved to {"action": "remove_row"} on original, the paper reports no replication outcome for it; the failed replication outcome belongs exclusively to the empirical target Riccucci, Van Ryzin, & Li (2016, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12401) in sibling row 541 and must not be borrowed for row 540.

decisions.quote:
Following this notion, the present study provides a wide replication (Walker et al., 2019) of the
original research by Riccucci et al. (2016). The preregistered survey experiment is set in the policy field of criminal
justice, a context that features the co-production of areas such as prisoner rehabilitation (Loeffler & Bovaird, 2020).
Applying the judicial system allows adding meaningful contextual variation to the design (Tsang & Kwan, 1999) by
testing the effects of symbolic representation in a context with greater organizational integration of the coproduction efforts (Nabatchi et al., 2017). This replication provides new data from a sample of 1000 citizens and
allows extending the original analytical strategy with robustness tests, such as a manipulation check.
decisions.reason: Under the verbatim Codebook Step 1 definition ('STEP 1 — RECORD TYPE: "record_type": "replication" if the paper collected new data or used a different sample to re-test a previously published finding; "reproduction" if it re-analysed the original study's own data (or code); "not_a_replication" if it re-tests no specific earlier published finding at all'), record_type ('type') is defined at the paper/record level, whereas Step 2 ('targets' / 'original') identifies which specific published work(s) the paper re-tests. Unlike single-row records where removing the sole shipped original means the paper re-tests no specific earlier published finding at all (making the paper-level record_type 'not_a_replication'), here the replicating paper (Sievert, 2021, DOI: 10.1111/padm.12743) collects new survey-experiment data from 1,000 German citizens to re-test a specific earlier published finding—namely Riccucci, Van Ryzin, & Li (2016, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12401), which is already captured in sibling row 541. Consequently, the paper-level record type is 'replication' (confirmed by both shipped row 540 and the blind coding), and the spurious background citation in row 540 is removed via Step 2 ('original': {"action": "remove_row"}) rather than by overriding the Step 1 paper-level type to 'not_a_replication'.
